topics.title: Design Calendar / Meeting Scheduler
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a calendar and meeting scheduler like Google Calendar. Asha wants a 45-minute meeting with Bilal and Chetan tomorrow in the Kaveri room. The system should show conflicts, never double-book the room, and suggest the first time all three are free.

Bilal's weekly standup is "every Monday 9:00 New York time" – which is 18:30 in Bengaluru one week and 19:30 the next, when US clocks change. Time zones are where calendar designs usually break.

## Requirements

- Create events with an organiser, attendees, a time slot and optionally a room.
- A room can never be booked for two overlapping events.
- Show a person's conflicts for a proposed time.
- Find the earliest slot of a given length when all attendees are free.
- Support weekly recurring events in the organiser's time zone.

## Step 1: Clarify the requirements

**Candidate:** Can people be double-booked?

**Interviewer:** Yes – show a warning, but let them decide. Rooms can't be.

**Candidate:** Do we need free-slot suggestions?

**Interviewer:** Yes: "first 45 minutes when everyone's free between 9:30 and 18:00".

**Candidate:** Recurring events?

**Interviewer:** Weekly is enough for now.

**Candidate:** Attendees in different time zones?

**Interviewer:** Yes – the team is in Bengaluru and New York.

**Candidate:** Is a meeting ending at 11:00 a conflict with one starting at 11:00?

**Interviewer:** No, back-to-back is fine.

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Settle three rules early: are slots half-open (end exclusive), can people be double-booked, and in which time zone does a recurring event repeat.

| Functional | Non-functional |
| --- | --- |
| Create events, rooms, attendees | Rooms never double-booked |
| Conflicts and free-slot search | Correct across time zones and DST |
| Weekly recurrence | Fast enough for a day's view |

## Step 2: Identify the core objects

- **Slot** – a time range `[start, end)` stored as `Instant`s.
- **Event** – title, organiser, attendees, slot, optional room.
- **WeeklyRule** – day of week, local start time, length and **time zone**; expands into slots.
- **CalendarService** – schedules events, checks room clashes, finds conflicts and free slots.

[![Selected design: a scheduling request goes to the calendar service, which checks the room's events for overlaps, stores the event on every attendee's calendar, reports personal conflicts, searches merged busy times for the first common free slot, and expands weekly rules using a time zone.](designs/lld-20.svg)](designs/lld-20.svg)

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Store every slot as an **`Instant`** (a point on the global timeline) and keep the **time zone with the rule**, not with the stored times. Comparisons are then always correct; local times appear only when displaying or expanding a rule.

## Step 3: Design the classes

### Slot

Two instants with `overlaps(other)`: `start < other.end && other.start < end`. Because the end is exclusive, 10:00–11:00 and 11:00–11:30 don't overlap.

### Event

An immutable record with the attendees and the optional room.

### WeeklyRule

Turns "every Monday 09:00 in America/New_York" into real instants week by week, letting Java's time zone rules handle daylight saving.

### CalendarService

Keeps events by person and by room. `schedule` refuses room overlaps; `conflictsFor` lists a person's overlapping events; `firstCommonFree` finds the earliest gap.

[![Class diagram: CalendarService keeps Events by person and by room; each Event has a Slot of two Instants, an organiser, attendees and an optional room; WeeklyRule has a day, a local start time, a length and a ZoneId and produces Slots.](learning-figures/lld-20-classes.svg)](learning-figures/lld-20-classes.svg)

## Step 4: Write the code

### Slot and Event

```java
/** A time range [start, end). Stored as Instants so time zones can't confuse comparisons. */
record Slot(Instant start, Instant end) {
    Slot {
        if (!start.isBefore(end)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("End before start");
    }
    boolean overlaps(Slot o) { return start.isBefore(o.end) && o.start.isBefore(end); }
}

record Event(String id, String title, String organizer, Set<String> attendees,
             Slot slot, String room) {}
```

### Weekly recurrence

```java
/** "Every Monday 10:00–10:30 in Asia/Kolkata", expanded into concrete slots. */
record WeeklyRule(DayOfWeek day, LocalTime start, Duration length, ZoneId zone) {
    List<Slot> occurrences(LocalDate from, int count) {
        List<Slot> out = new ArrayList<>();
        LocalDate d = from;
        while (d.getDayOfWeek() != day) d = d.plusDays(1);
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++, d = d.plusWeeks(1)) {
            Instant s = ZonedDateTime.of(d, start, zone).toInstant();  // local → instant
            out.add(new Slot(s, s.plus(length)));
        }
        return out;
    }
}
```

### CalendarService

```java
class CalendarService {
    private final Map<String, List<Event>> byPerson = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, List<Event>> byRoom = new HashMap<>();
    private int nextId = 1;

    /** Rooms can't be double-booked; people get a warning-free invite (they decide). */
    synchronized Event schedule(String title, String organizer, Set<String> attendees,
                                Slot slot, String room) {
        if (room != null && byRoom.getOrDefault(room, List.of()).stream()
                .anyMatch(e -> e.slot().overlaps(slot)))
            throw new IllegalStateException(room + " is already booked then");
        Event e = new Event("EV-" + nextId++, title, organizer, Set.copyOf(attendees),
                slot, room);
        Set<String> everyone = new HashSet<>(attendees);
        everyone.add(organizer);
        everyone.forEach(p -> byPerson.computeIfAbsent(p, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e));
        if (room != null) byRoom.computeIfAbsent(room, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e);
        return e;
    }

    List<Event> conflictsFor(String person, Slot slot) {
        return byPerson.getOrDefault(person, List.of()).stream()
                .filter(e -> e.slot().overlaps(slot)).toList();
    }

    /** Earliest gap of `length` inside `window` when everyone is free. */
    Optional<Slot> firstCommonFree(Set<String> people, Slot window, Duration length) {
        List<Slot> busy = people.stream()
                .flatMap(p -> byPerson.getOrDefault(p, List.of()).stream())
                .map(Event::slot)
                .filter(s -> s.overlaps(window))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Slot::start))
                .toList();
        Instant cursor = window.start();
        for (Slot b : busy) {
            if (!cursor.plus(length).isAfter(b.start()))            // gap before this meeting
                return Optional.of(new Slot(cursor, cursor.plus(length)));
            if (b.end().isAfter(cursor)) cursor = b.end();          // skip past this meeting
        }
        Instant end = cursor.plus(length);
        if (end.isAfter(window.end())) return Optional.empty();
        return Optional.of(new Slot(cursor, end));
    }
}
```

### Worked example

Wednesday 28 Oct 2026, times in IST.

| Step | Request | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Asha: Design review 10:00–11:00 with Bilal, room Kaveri | Booked |
| 2 | Bilal: 1:1 with Chetan 11:30–12:00, no room | Booked |
| 3 | Chetan: Standup 10:30–10:45 in Kaveri | **Refused** – Kaveri busy |
| 4 | Bilal's conflicts for 10:30–11:45 | 2 (design review, 1:1) |
| 5 | Bilal's conflicts for 11:00–11:30 | none – back-to-back is fine |
| 6 | First common 45 min, 09:30–18:00 | **12:00–12:45** (09:30–10:00 is only 30 min) |
| 7 | First common 30 min | **09:30–10:00** |
| 8 | Weekly standup, Mon 09:00 New York | 26 Oct → 18:30 IST; 2 Nov → **19:30 IST** (US clocks changed) |

### Edge cases

| Case | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| End before start | Rejected |
| Meeting spanning midnight | Fine – instants don't care about dates |
| No common gap in the window | `Optional.empty()` |
| Organiser not in attendees | Added to the organiser's calendar anyway |

## Step 5: The free-slot algorithm

To find the first gap of 45 minutes for Asha, Bilal and Chetan:

1. Collect everyone's busy slots inside the window and **sort them by start**: 10:00–11:00, 10:00–11:00, 11:30–12:00, 11:30–12:00.
2. Start a cursor at the window start, 09:30.
3. For each busy slot: if `cursor + 45 min` fits before it starts, that's the answer. Otherwise move the cursor to the end of that busy slot (if later).
4. 09:30 + 45 = 10:15 > 10:00 → no; cursor → 11:00. 11:45 > 11:30 → no; cursor → 12:00.
5. No more meetings: 12:00–12:45 fits inside the window → answer.

This is the classic "merge intervals" idea: sort once, sweep once – O(n log n).

![Animation: busy meetings for three people are sorted on a timeline; a cursor starts at 9:30 and needs 45 minutes; the gap before 10:00 is too short so the cursor jumps to 11:00; the gap before 11:30 is too short so it jumps to 12:00; there the 45-minute slot from 12:00 to 12:45 fits.](learning-figures/lld-20-freeslot.gif)

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Storing recurring events as "UTC 13:00 every Monday". When the organiser's country changes its clocks, the meeting silently moves by an hour in their own time. Store the local time **and** the zone ID, and expand with time-zone rules.

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Room booking across servers needs the same atomic check as any booking: a database exclusion constraint (PostgreSQL `EXCLUDE USING gist` on room + time range) makes overlapping room bookings impossible.

## Step 6: Deep dives

### Invitations and responses

Add an `Invitation` per attendee with status (pending, accepted, declined, tentative). Free-slot search can ignore events the person declined.

### Full recurrence rules

Real calendars use iCalendar RRULEs ("every 2nd Tuesday", "last weekday of the month") and exceptions ("skip 25 Dec", "move this one to 11:00"). Store the rule plus a list of exceptions, and expand only the range being viewed.

### Fast day and week views

Keep each person's events in a sorted structure (a `TreeMap` by start, or a database index on (person, start)), so "events this week" is a range query.

### Working hours and time zones per person

Each user has a zone and working hours; the free-slot search intersects the window with every attendee's working hours, converted to instants.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**Why half-open intervals?** So back-to-back meetings don't conflict and adjacent slots tile perfectly with no gaps or overlaps.

**Why not store local date-times?** "10:00" means different moments in Bengaluru and New York. Instants are unambiguous; local times are for display and for rules.

**How do you handle a 500-person all-hands?** Store the event once and reference it from attendees, rather than copying it 500 times; free-slot search for 500 people is rarely needed.

**How would you suggest several options, not just the first?** Keep sweeping after the first match and collect up to N gaps, maybe preferring mid-morning.

## Wrap up

Slots are half-open ranges of instants; rooms are protected by an overlap check; free slots come from sorting busy times and sweeping; recurring events keep their local time and zone and are expanded with time-zone rules.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Store instants; keep the zone with the recurrence rule.
> - Half-open intervals: back-to-back is not a conflict.
> - Rooms are booked atomically; people may be double-booked with a warning.
> - Free-slot search = sort busy slots, sweep with a cursor.

## Going deeper (optional)

The complete, runnable code is [CalendarDemo.java](reference-code/learning/kb/calendar/CalendarDemo.java). It replays the worked example, including the New York daylight-saving change, and checks every result.

[![Expand recurring occurrences using a timezone identifier and policy.](lessons/lld-20-failure.svg)](lessons/lld-20-failure.svg)

## Closing answer

"A Slot is a half-open range of two Instants, so comparisons are time-zone-proof and back-to-back meetings don't conflict. An Event has an organiser, attendees, a slot and an optional room. The CalendarService indexes events by person and by room: scheduling refuses any overlap in the room – across servers that's a database exclusion constraint – while personal overlaps are shown as conflicts. To find a common free slot I collect everyone's busy slots in the window, sort them by start and sweep a cursor until a gap of the required length fits. Recurring events store the local time and the zone ID and are expanded with Java's time-zone rules, so a 9:00 New York standup correctly moves from 18:30 to 19:30 in India when US clocks change."

topics.title: Large-scale API Gateway
topics.concepts: Routing, authentication, rate limiting, load balancing, observability
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a large-scale API gateway like Kong, AWS API Gateway, Zuul or an Envoy-based edge. Every request from the mobile app – `GET /orders/5521`, `POST /payments` – enters through the gateway, which checks who is calling, applies limits, and forwards the request to the right one of 300 backend services.

Because everything passes through it, the gateway must be very fast, must never become the outage, and must stop one slow backend from dragging the others down.

## Requirements

- Route requests to backend services by host, path and version.
- Authenticate callers (JWT, API keys) and pass identity to backends.
- Rate-limit per client and per route.
- Protect backends: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers.
- Change routes and policies without restarts; add little latency (a few ms).

## Step 1: Clarify the requirements

> **💡 Tip**
> Split the gateway into a **data plane** (handles every request, must be fast) and a **control plane** (manages configuration, can be slower). This is the key idea.

**Candidate:** What traffic volume?

**Interviewer:** 1 million requests per second at peak, across regions.

**Candidate:** How many backend services and routes?

**Interviewer:** About 300 services, 5,000 routes.

**Candidate:** Which authentication?

**Interviewer:** OAuth2 JWTs for users, API keys for partners.

**Candidate:** How quickly must route changes take effect?

**Interviewer:** Within about 30 seconds, without dropping requests.

**Candidate:** What latency budget?

**Interviewer:** Under 5 ms added at p99.

**Functional requirements**

1. Route, authenticate, rate-limit, transform headers.
2. Timeouts, retries and circuit breaking per backend.
3. Dynamic configuration; metrics, logs and traces.

**Non-functional requirements**

1. 1 million requests/s, under 5 ms added latency.
2. Highly available: no single point of failure.
3. Bad configuration must never take the gateway down.

## Step 2: Estimate the scale

> **💡 Tip**
> Gateway nodes are CPU-bound (TLS, parsing). Size by requests per core.

```text
Peak traffic            = 1,000,000 requests/s
Per gateway node        ≈ 20,000 requests/s (16 cores, TLS)
Nodes                   = 1M / 20,000 = 50 → ~75 with headroom, spread over 3 regions
Config                  = 5,000 routes × 2 KB ≈ 10 MB (fits in memory on every node)
```

What it means: the gateway is a horizontally scaled, stateless fleet; all routing configuration lives in each node's memory.

## Step 3: Define the API

The data plane has no API of its own – it proxies:

```http
GET https://api.example.com/v2/orders/5521
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…
→ forwarded to http://orders-v2.internal/orders/5521
   with headers: X-User-Id: asha, X-Request-Id: 9f2c…, traceparent: …
```

The control plane has an admin API:

```http
PUT /admin/routes/orders-v2
{ "match": { "host": "api.example.com", "pathPrefix": "/v2/orders" },
  "upstream": "orders-v2", "timeoutMs": 800, "retries": 1,
  "rateLimit": { "perClient": "100/s" }, "auth": "jwt" }
```

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Say that backends trust identity headers only from the gateway – on a private network or with mutual TLS – so a client cannot forge `X-User-Id`.

## Step 4: Define the data model

| Store | Contents | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Route and policy config | routes, upstreams, auth and limit settings, version | Control-plane database (etcd / Postgres), pushed to every node's memory |
| Rate-limit counters | client + route → tokens | Local per node, plus Redis for global limits |
| Upstream health | instance → healthy / ejected | In memory on each node, from active and passive checks |
| JWT signing keys | issuer → public keys | Cached in memory, refreshed periodically |

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Each node keeps a complete **snapshot** of configuration in memory. The request path never calls the control plane, so a control-plane outage does not stop traffic.

## Step 5: Draw the high-level design

[![High-level design: clients call the gateway data plane, which applies the in-memory policy snapshot and forwards to upstream services through per-dependency bulkheads; the control plane validates and publishes new snapshots; every node sends telemetry.](designs/hld-20.svg)](designs/hld-20.svg)

**One request**

1. Asha's app calls `GET /v2/orders/5521`. A load balancer sends it to any gateway node.
2. The node terminates TLS and finds the route in its in-memory table.
3. It validates the JWT locally with cached public keys.
4. It checks the rate limit for Asha's client on this route.
5. It forwards to a healthy `orders-v2` instance with an 800 ms timeout, adding identity and trace headers.
6. It records metrics, an access log line and a trace span.

**Changing configuration**

1. An engineer updates the route through the admin API.
2. The control plane validates it and publishes a new snapshot version.
3. Nodes receive the snapshot, check it, and swap it in atomically; in-flight requests finish on the old one.

![Animation: a request passes through the gateway's filters one by one – TLS, route match, JWT check, rate limit – and is forwarded to the orders service; a second client over its limit is stopped at the rate-limit filter with 429 before reaching any backend.](learning-figures/hld-20-filters.gif)

## Step 6: Go deep

### Rate limiting across 75 nodes: the algorithm

**Option 1: Exact global counter in Redis for every request.**

- Good: precise.
- Problem: a Redis call on every request adds latency and makes Redis critical.

**Option 2: Local limits per node (global limit ÷ number of nodes).**

- Good: no network call.
- Problem: uneven load balancing makes it imprecise.

**Option 3: Local token buckets that sync with a shared store every few hundred milliseconds.**

- Good: fast and close to exact.
- Problem: can overshoot briefly.

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Local token buckets with periodic sync for most routes; an exact Redis check only for expensive or paid partner limits. (See the Rate Limiter lesson, HLD-2.)

### Protecting backends

- **Timeouts per route:** never wait forever.
- **Retries only for safe requests** (GET, or POST with an idempotency key), with a retry budget – for example at most 10% extra traffic.
- **Circuit breaker:** if `payments` fails 50% of requests for 10 seconds, stop sending to it for a short time and fail fast.
- **Bulkheads:** a limited pool of connections per backend, so a slow `reports` service cannot use up every connection and starve `orders`.

[![Protecting backends: each upstream has its own connection pool; requests get a timeout; failures feed a circuit breaker; when the payments service keeps failing the breaker opens and requests fail fast instead of piling up, while the orders service is unaffected.](learning-figures/hld-20-protect.svg)](learning-figures/hld-20-protect.svg)

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Retrying everything at every layer. If the app, the gateway and the service each retry 3 times, one failure becomes 27 calls – the retries cause the outage.

### Safe configuration rollout

A bad route (a typo that matches every path) could break the whole API in seconds. So the control plane validates the config, deploys it to a few canary nodes first, watches error rates, then rolls out everywhere. Nodes keep the last good snapshot and refuse an invalid one.

### Keep the gateway thin

Business logic (aggregating three services into one response) belongs in backend services or a backend-for-frontend, not in the shared gateway. A fat gateway becomes every team's bottleneck.

## Step 7: Find bottlenecks and failure points

| What fails | What happens | How we handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control plane is down | No config changes | Nodes keep serving from their last snapshot |
| A bad config is published | Could break all traffic | Validation, canary rollout, keep last good snapshot |
| One backend becomes slow | Connections pile up | Timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breaker |
| A client floods the API | Others slowed | Per-client rate limits return 429 |
| A gateway node dies | Its requests fail | Load balancer health checks remove it; stateless nodes |

## Putting it together

- **Data plane:** stateless nodes; TLS → route → auth → limit → forward with timeouts, all from memory.
- **Control plane:** validate, version and publish snapshots; canary rollout.
- **Resilience:** bulkheads, circuit breakers, retry budgets, last-good config.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**API gateway vs service mesh?** The gateway handles north-south traffic (clients into the system); a mesh (Envoy sidecars) handles east-west traffic between services. They share many features.

**How do you do canary releases of a backend?** A route sends 5% of traffic to `orders-v3` and 95% to `orders-v2`, adjusted by weight in the config.

**How do you avoid a JWT validation call per request?** Validate signatures locally with cached public keys (JWKS), refreshed every few minutes.

**Where does TLS terminate?** At the gateway (or the load balancer in front); traffic to backends uses mutual TLS inside the network.

## Wrap up

We split the gateway into a fast, stateless data plane that works from an in-memory snapshot, and a control plane that validates and rolls out configuration safely.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Data plane vs control plane: the request path never waits on configuration.
> - Validate JWTs and rate-limit locally to keep added latency in milliseconds.
> - Timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breakers and retry budgets protect backends.
> - Roll configuration out like code: validate, canary, keep the last good version.

## Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version shows how to validate and publish a snapshot atomically so every node either uses the new version or keeps the last good one.

[![Routing and resilience preserve downstream capacity and caller identity.](lessons/hld-20-flow.svg)](lessons/hld-20-flow.svg)

Further reading: [Envoy architecture overview](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/arch_overview) and [Spring Cloud Gateway](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-gateway/reference/).

## Closing answer

"I split the gateway into a data plane and a control plane. Data-plane nodes are stateless and scaled horizontally behind a load balancer; each holds the full route and policy snapshot in memory. A request is matched to a route, its JWT is validated locally with cached keys, it is rate-limited with local token buckets synced to a shared store, and it is forwarded with identity and trace headers, a per-route timeout, a bulkhead per upstream, a circuit breaker and a strict retry budget. The control plane validates configuration, publishes versioned snapshots and rolls them out by canary; nodes keep the last good snapshot, so a control-plane outage or a bad config never stops traffic."

topics.title: Spring AI Master Project
topics.concepts: Enterprise Agent + RAG + MCP + tools + memory + observability
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Capstone: build **ShopEasy Help**, an enterprise support assistant with Spring AI. Asha can ask policy questions ("What's the return window for electronics?"), ask about her own orders ("Where is 5521?"), and request actions ("Return the headphones from that order") – in one conversation that remembers context.

This lesson puts together everything from the AI track – prompts, structured output, RAG, memory, advisors, tools, evaluation, security and production architecture – into one design you can build and explain end to end.

## Requirements

- Answer policy questions from approved documents, with citations (RAG).
- Answer questions about the user's own orders and start returns (tools).
- Remember the conversation (memory), scoped to the logged-in user.
- Enforce permissions and confirmations in code; validate outputs.
- Be measurable: tracing, cost tracking and an evaluation gate before releases.

## Step 1: The idea in plain words

The assistant is a normal Spring Boot service with a `ChatClient` at its centre. Around it, each concern you've learned is one well-defined piece:

| Need | Building block | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear behaviour | System prompt, low temperature | AI-2, AI-3 |
| Policy answers | Ingestion + vector store + `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` | AI-5, AI-10 |
| Context across turns | `ChatMemory` + `MessageChatMemoryAdvisor` | AI-9 |
| Cross-cutting rules | Advisors (masking, logging) | AI-12 |
| Orders and returns | `@Tool` methods with `ToolContext` | AI-13 |
| Typed results | Structured output (`entity()`) | AI-8 |
| Safety | Permission-scoped retrieval, confirmations | AI-18 |
| Quality and cost | Tracing, evaluation set, budgets | AI-17, AI-19 |

> **🎯 In the interview**
> For a capstone or "design an AI assistant" question, interviewers want to see that you can combine these pieces, explain the request flow, and say what you'd build first and how you'd know it works.

## Step 2: The architecture and one request's execution

[![Selected design: an ingestion service builds the approved evidence index; the assistant API receives questions and loads conversation history; the ChatClient pipeline adds memory and retrieved policies and can call the authorized order tool; evaluation and operations measure quality, cost and latency.](designs/ai-20.svg)](designs/ai-20.svg)

One conversation:

1. **"What's the return window for electronics?"** → memory (empty) + RAG retrieves *Returns Policy v6 §2* → *"10 days from delivery for electronics [Returns Policy §2]."*
2. **"Is my order 5521 still returnable?"** → the model calls `getOrder("5521")`; the tool checks Asha owns it → delivered 4 days ago → *"Yes, you have 6 days left."*
3. **"Return the headphones from that order."** → memory resolves "that order" = 5521 → the model calls `prepareReturn("5521", "headphones")` → the tool creates a **draft** return → *"I've prepared a return for the headphones (₹2,499). Please confirm."*
4. Asha taps **Confirm** in the UI → the app (not the model) submits the return.

![Animation: three turns of one conversation – a policy question answered from the returns policy with a citation, an order question answered by the getOrder tool after an ownership check, and a return request that memory links to the same order and the prepareReturn tool turns into a draft that Asha confirms in the app.](learning-figures/ai-20-conversation.gif)

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> The model never performs the final irreversible action. It prepares a draft; a button the user clicks – handled by ordinary application code – commits it.

## Step 3: In code with Spring AI

**The assistant service** – one `ChatClient` with memory, RAG, logging and tools:

```java
@Service
public class ShopEasyHelp {
    private final ChatClient chatClient;
    private final OrderTools orderTools;

    public ShopEasyHelp(ChatClient.Builder builder, ChatMemory memory,
                        VectorStore policies, OrderTools orderTools) {
        this.orderTools = orderTools;
        this.chatClient = builder
                .defaultSystem("""
                        You are ShopEasy Help. Answer policy questions only from the provided
                        context and cite the section. Use tools for order questions.
                        Never claim an action is done unless a tool result says so.""")
                .defaultOptions(ChatOptions.builder().temperature(0.2).maxTokens(600).build())
                .defaultAdvisors(
                        MessageChatMemoryAdvisor.builder(memory).build(),
                        QuestionAnswerAdvisor.builder(policies)
                                .searchRequest(SearchRequest.builder().topK(4)
                                        .similarityThreshold(0.6)
                                        .filterExpression("status == 'PUBLISHED'").build())
                                .build(),
                        new SimpleLoggerAdvisor())
                .build();
    }

    public String chat(User user, String chatId, String message) {
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .user(message)
                .tools(orderTools)
                .toolContext(Map.of("user", user))
                .advisors(a -> a.param(ChatMemory.CONVERSATION_ID, user.id() + ":" + chatId))
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}
```

**The tools** – identity from `ToolContext`, drafts instead of irreversible actions:

```java
@Component
public class OrderTools {
    private final OrderService orders;
    private final ReturnService returns;

    public OrderTools(OrderService orders, ReturnService returns) {
        this.orders = orders; this.returns = returns;
    }

    @Tool(description = "Get one of the current user's orders: items, status, delivery date")
    public OrderView getOrder(@ToolParam(description = "Order number") String orderId,
                              ToolContext ctx) {
        return orders.viewFor(user(ctx), orderId);              // throws if not the user's order
    }

    @Tool(description = "Prepare a return for an item; the user must confirm it in the app")
    public ReturnDraft prepareReturn(@ToolParam(description = "Order number") String orderId,
                                     @ToolParam(description = "Item name") String item,
                                     ToolContext ctx) {
        return returns.draftFor(user(ctx), orderId, item);      // checks the return window
    }

    private User user(ToolContext ctx) { return (User) ctx.getContext().get("user"); }
}
```

**The confirm endpoint** – plain Spring MVC, no model involved:

```java
@PostMapping("/returns/{draftId}/confirm")
ReturnResult confirm(@PathVariable String draftId, @AuthenticationPrincipal User user) {
    return returns.confirm(user, draftId);                      // idempotent
}
```

## Step 4: Common mistakes

| Mistake | Better |
| --- | --- |
| Building everything at once | Milestones: RAG answers → memory → read-only tools → draft actions → evaluation gate |
| The model "does" the return | The model drafts; the user confirms; app code commits |
| Conversation ID from the client | `userId + chatId` from the session |
| Old policy versions retrieved | Ingest with version and status; filter to PUBLISHED |
| No evaluation until launch | Build the evaluation set in week one and grow it |
| Not checking the final prompt size | Memory + RAG + tool results share one budget |

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Letting the model's text decide policy, such as "the return window is 15 days" from an old chunk. The **tool** checks the real return window from the order system; the model only explains it.

## Step 5: Production concerns

- **Evaluation set** (AI-17): 150 cases – policy questions, order questions, multi-turn references ("that order"), out-of-scope questions, injection attempts and other users' order numbers. Gate releases on correctness, citation accuracy and zero security failures.
- **Observability:** trace every turn with prompt version, retrieved sections, tool calls, tokens and cost.
- **Cost:** about 3,000 input tokens per turn (system + memory + 4 chunks); route simple FAQs to a smaller model once evaluation allows (AI-19).
- **Security:** permission-scoped retrieval, ownership checks in every tool, confirmations, output encoding (AI-18).
- **Rollout:** internal staff first, then 5% of customers, watching escalations and thumbs-down rates.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**What would you build first?** Policy Q&A with RAG and citations, plus the evaluation set. It delivers value with no write access and teaches you about your documents.

**How do you handle "talk to a human"?** A tool or UI action that creates a support ticket with the conversation summary attached.

**How do you keep answers consistent with live data?** Facts that change per order come from tools at answer time; documents give general rules; the model combines them.

**How would you scale it?** Stateless app instances, memory in a database, vector store and model calls behind the AI gateway with budgets and fallbacks.

## Wrap up

ShopEasy Help is one `ChatClient` combining memory, permission-scoped RAG and user-scoped tools, with drafts for actions, confirmations in app code, and evaluation, tracing and budgets around it.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Each concern is a separate, testable piece: prompt, RAG, memory, advisors, tools.
> - Identity and permissions come from the session, enforced in code.
> - The model drafts actions; the user confirms; the app commits.
> - Build in milestones and gate every release on an evaluation set.

## Closing answer

"ShopEasy Help is a Spring Boot service built around one ChatClient. Policy documents are ingested with versions and status into a vector store, and `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` retrieves published sections so answers cite them. `MessageChatMemoryAdvisor` keeps the conversation, keyed by the authenticated user and chat. Order questions use `@Tool` methods that take the user from `ToolContext` and check ownership; actions like returns are only drafted by a tool and committed when the user confirms in the app, with an idempotent endpoint. Prompts are versioned, temperature is low and output tokens capped. Every turn is traced with tokens and cost, and releases are gated on an evaluation set covering policy, orders, multi-turn references, out-of-scope questions and security cases."
